Chapter 5. Preparation, Contingency Planning, and Learning from Experience.
You know, real success—whether it’s on the battlefield or in the boardroom—almost never comes down to simple luck. It’s built on careful preparation, smart backup plans, and a genuine commitment to learning from everything that happens. These are the habits that create organizations able to bounce back from setbacks and grab opportunities as soon as they show up.
So, where does it all start? Preparation. This means really understanding what you’ve got—your strengths, your resources, your limits. In the military, that’s making sure everyone’s trained up, equipment’s ready, and logistics are solid. In business, it’s about building your team’s skills, investing in the right technology, and setting up processes that let you stay flexible and creative.
Next up is contingency planning. Basically, it’s about asking, “What could go wrong—and what are we gonna do about it?” Military teams are always thinking through a handful of backup plans, weighing out the best-case, worst-case, and what’s most likely to happen. Businesses should do the same—think about risks like supply chain hiccups, new regulations, or changing customer needs, and map out ways to deal with them.
Here’s a simple framework to help you build strong contingency plans:
First, identify critical risks. What could really throw your plans off track? Second, assess both the likelihood and the impact. How likely are these risks, and how bad would it be if they actually happened? Third, develop response plans. What steps will you take if something does go sideways? And finally, assign responsibilities. Who’s in charge of keeping an eye on each risk, and who jumps in if something goes wrong?
When teams think these things through ahead of time, they’re able to react faster and with more confidence when a challenge pops up. That means less chaos, smoother transitions, and a much better shot at keeping things moving forward.
Now, there’s one more piece to this puzzle: learning from experience. In the military, folks do after-action reviews to break down what happened, why it happened, and how they can do even better next time. Businesses should definitely take a page from that playbook. When teams make it a habit to reflect—really look at what worked and what didn’t—they start to spot best practices, stop making the same mistakes, and keep raising their game.
Imagine a company rolls out a new product, but runs into technical problems nobody saw coming. If they take the time to honestly review what happened, they might find gaps in their testing process—and then fix them, so it doesn’t happen again. Over time, this kind of commitment to learning creates a culture where every setback is just another chance to get stronger, not something to hide away.
Here’s the big takeaway: preparation, contingency planning, and learning aren’t just things you do once and forget about. They’re ongoing habits—practices that demand discipline, humility, and the guts to adapt as things change.
When leaders weave these habits into the daily life of their teams, they build organizations that don’t just survive tough times—they actually find ways to thrive, no matter how uncertain the world gets.
